title: Drowning The Hippo Attack | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We've seen e3 before, and the response is d5. This looks like a Hippo setup — g3, e3, then b3 and d3.
Against all of these flank defences, the best plan is to occupy the centre — e5.
The effective anti-Hippo setup starts with the knight to f6...
...and then c6, which I really like — it builds a pawn chain so his fianchettoed bishop bites on granite.
That pawn triangle, just like in the London, gives the bishop a home on d6.
You might ask where the queen's knight goes now that c6 is taken — the answer is d7.
The knight to d7 — heading, ultimately, toward the kingside to feed an attack. Not c5, where it would walk into d4 and do nothing.
The knight reroutes, f8 then g6 — Ruy Lopez style.
What is that knight doing? It sits on the kingside — so future sacrifices are in the air, and it makes the h5-then-h4 storm much more effective.
Since we're attacking on the kingside, close the centre — e4. If he plays c4 it achieves nothing; the pawn on d5 is very well protected.
A common misconception is that we must develop the bishop. We don't — it's perfectly happy on c8, and we'll bring it out only when we need it. Play h5; we're going for the king.
c4 accomplishes nothing.
The pawn on d5 is well protected, so h4 — we're already on the verge of delivering mate. That's how fast this is.

Recapture on d5. His knight to c3 accomplishes nothing. Now be careful how we open the kingside — hxg3 is double-edged, since after fxg3 he opens the f-file for his rook, so we need a follow-up. Don't hurry: the tempting knight to e4 hits h2, but it's wrong — it gives up the pawn on d5, and if d5 falls, the e4-pawn goes with it.
One prophylactic move first — the bishop to e6. It defends the pawn on d5 and clears the way for a future knight to g4. These are exactly the quiet moves people hate to play when they're attacking.
If he's angling for the knight to b5, we can always retreat the bishop to b8. Now the time has come to open fire on the kingside.
hxg3, and the knight to g4.

Notice his bishop is overloaded — defending both d5 and the knight. He grabs on d5, but I'd planned for this: his knight is now hanging, and if we move ours with tempo, he'll have two loose pieces at once.
Not taking on f3 — that just drops the knight. The knight takes on h2, hitting the rook: if it moves, we win the other knight. It isn't fully clear-cut, since his knight can return to c3.
He finds the knight to f4, also a good move.
We take the rook.
Now we're up the exchange, and still attacking.
Trade on f4 to remove his knight.

He recaptures, and we've converted the attack into material — an extra exchange. Now the technique: f5 is one way, but it allows d5, opening his bishop's diagonal, so this must be handled very carefully.
f5 — defending the e4-pawn, which feels like the most important pawn on the board.
It also shuts his bishop out of the game. He answers d5 — he's good.
We retreat the bishop to f7.
He takes on g7 — the question I was weighing is whether that pawn is worth giving up.
And it is worth it — because we keep the e4-pawn, which is enormous.
The bishop to h6 is a mistake — a losing move. Whenever the king on g1 is this weak, be hyper-aware of every route to it, on both wings — and the f2-square is the sensitive one.
The bishop to c5 with check is guarded, but the queen to b6 with check forces his king onto the h-file — and there sits his undefended bishop on h6. We swing the rook to h8 and collect it.
My technique here was a touch sloppy — the bishop to d4 was not actually so clear.
The rook to g6 doesn't trap the bishop, because of bishop g5. The rook to h8 is better — it pins.

Convert as fast as possible: his knight on h2 is very vulnerable, so double on the h-file — walk the king to e7 and bring the other rook to h8. We're not afraid of him grabbing on c4; he's out of pieces and our king is safe in the centre. And there's even a forced mate: once his queen leaves e2 and the bishop is gone from g2, the f2-square lights up — take on h2, swing the rook to the h-file, and after the block, crash into f2.
